back: The distance a vehicle travels under the braking force. This can be affected by adverse road and weather conditions as well as the condition of the vehicle.

front: Which forces require contact between objects, and which don't?

Contact forces: friction, air-resistance (air is an object) normal force
Non-contact forces: weight, electrostatic force, magnetic force

reaction times are in the range of 0.2-0.9 seconds.

front: Explain what is meant by a scalar quantity. Give 2 examples
back:
A scalar quantity is a quantity with a magnitude, but no direction.
E.g. distance, speed, time, mass, energy..

front: Explain what is meant by a vector quantity. Give 2 examples
back:
A vector quantity has both a magnitude and a direction.
E.g. Force, velocity, displacement, momentum, moment...

front:
Which property of a distance-time graph

back:
A = constant speed

B = at rest

C = accelerating

front:
What is meant by acceleration?
Give its unit.
back: A vector quantity that is the change in velocity per unit of time. Unit is m/s2

Which property of a velocity-time graph can be used
to calculate acceleration?
back: Gradient (slope)

front:
Which property of a velocity-time graph can be used
to calculate distance travelled?
back: Area under the graph

front: For the v-t graphs given below, decide which one is accelerating; moving with constant speed or decelerating
back:
A = constant speed
B = accelerating
C = decelerating

front: Name two types of forces that always oppose motion
back:
1. Friction
2. Air Resistance (Drag)

front: Which type of force holds planets around the Sun?
back: Gravitational Force

front: Which type of force holds electrons around nucleus?
back: Electrostatic Force

front: State three ways a force can affect an object
back:
- It can change the shape of the object (extension/compression)
- It can change the speed of the object
- It can change the direction the object is moving

front:
What factors that affect the stopping distance
of a car?
back:
- Reaction time
- Weather conditions
- Initial speed
- Driver’s conditions
- Road Conditions
- Mass of the car
- Tire Conditions

front:
State two factors that affect the air

back:
- Surface Area
- Speed

front: Explain what is the difference between elastic and plastic behavior.
back:
In elastic behaviour, object recovers its original shape when the forces causing the extension is removed.

In plastic behavior, there is a permanent deformation to the shape of the object when forces are removed.
Current flow consisting of charges that continually change direction.

Current flow consisting of charges flowing in a single direction only.
The green and yellow wire connected to metal casings of appliances, that prevents an appliance from becoming live.

a single closed loop. In metals, the charges that flow are electrons.

A light emitting component consisting of an enclosed metal filament. Its
resistance increases as the filament’s temperature increases.

front: What is a fuse and where is it placed?
back:
A safety device consisting of a thin metal filament that melts and cuts off the power
supply if there is a surge in current grater than its rating value, e.g. 5A. Fuses are connected to the live wire.
A material that doesn’t allow electrical charge to flow.

A light sensitive component whose resistance decreases
as its temperature increases.

A device that gives out light when a current flows through it. Current
can only flow through it in one direction, and a minimum voltage must be applied across it
before it illuminates.
The brown wire that carries the current from the supply to the appliance.
An a.c supply, which in the UK has a frequency of 50Hz a value of 230V.
The blue wire that completes the circuit in a mains power supply

A conductor whose current flow is directly proportional to the potential
difference (voltage) across it, when held at a constant temperature.
The unit of resistance.

directly proportional to the potential difference (voltage) across it.
Components connected in parallel have the same potential difference (voltage) across each component. The total current is equal to the sum of the currents flowing through each component.
The energy that is transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit. It is often also called a voltage
A measure of the opposition to current flow

front: What happens to total resistance in parallel?
back: The total resistance is less than the lowest individual resistance.

front: How do you calculate total resistance of resistors in series?
back: The total resistance is equal to the sum of the resistances of the individual resistors.

Components are connected in a single line, so the same current passes through each
component.

A temperature dependent component, whose resistance increases as its
temperature decreases.

The unit of power.

front: Describe the structure of the atom, including particle names and charges.
back: The atom has a positively charged nucleus which is made up of protons (+1) and neutrons (0). The nucleus is surrounded by electrons (-1), which all orbit the nucleus at different distances.

front: This symbol represents a cell. Which side is the positive terminal?
back: Left side (longer side)

front: How is a thermistor affected by changes in temperature?
back:
As temperature increases, its resistance
decreases
Potential difference

front:
What are the differences between series
and parallel circuits in regards to current
and voltage?
back:
In series:
- The same current flows through all the components
- The potential difference across the components is not the same. The total potential difference is equal to the sum of potential differences across each component.

In parallel:
- The sum of the currents in each section is equal to the total current.

- The potential difference across each branch is the same.

front: What is an voltmeter and where must it be connected in a circuit?
back: A device that is connected in parallel with a component to measure the potential difference (voltage) across it.

front: State what a Volt is equivalent to in other units.
back: Joule per Coulomb

front:
What is an ammeter and where must it
be connected in a circuit?
back:
An ammeter measures current. It is
placed in series with the component it is
required to measured.

front: What are the two things needed for a continuous current to flow?
back: A potential difference (voltage) and a closed circuit

front:
How does changing the resistance in a
circuit change the current?
back:
● Current is inversely proportional to resistance. Therefore at a constant voltage, increasing the resistance will decrease the current.

● In an electrical circuit the flow of electrons causes a current. A high resistance makes it harder for electrons to pass through and therefore reduces the current.

front:
How can you use a variable resistor to
increase the current in a series circuit?
back:
You set the variable resistor to have a
lower resistance, this should increase
the current.

front:
Explain the relationship between voltage,
current and resistance in a filament
lamp.
back:
As temperature increases in the lamp, the resistance also increases. This is because a higher temperature makes the atoms in the filament vibrate more, making it harder for electrons to pass through. This therefore decreases the current.

A filament lamp is not ohmic, meaning that current is not directly proportional to the potential difference. If voltage is double, current will not be doubled since there will be an increase in resistance

front: What electrical component does this graph represent?
back: Diode

front:
When an electrical current flows through
a resistor why does it heat up?
back:
There are collisions between the electrons and
the ions in the resistor’s lattice. This causes a
transfer of kinetic energy into thermal energy,
which is released into the surroundings.

front:
How do low resistance wires reduce
unwanted energy transfers?
back:
A smaller resistance will mean there are
fewer collisions, therefore less energy
will be wasted through heating.

front:
What are some advantages and
disadvantages of the heating effect?
back:
Advantages:
- Can be used for appliances such as toasters or electrical fires, where the hot wire helps heat the bread or room

Disadvantages:
- The loss of energy as heat energy can make an appliance inefficient
- If an appliance overheats it can catch fire or overheat, which could ruin the device or injure the user

front: Two voltage-time graphs are given below. Decide which one supplies D.C and which one supplied A.C
back:
A = Alternating Current
B = Direct Current

front:
What type of current do batteries and
cells supply?
back: Direct current.

front: How does an earth wire ensure safety?
back:
The earth wire is connected to the metal casing
of the device and provides a low resistance path
to the ground. Therefore if a fault occurs the
earth wire allows the large currents in the live
wire to flow through to the ground.

front:
Why is it important to connect a fuse or
switch to the live wire?
back:
When the switch is turned off, or when the fuse
breaks, it will break the circuit and stop current
running through the wire since live wire carries
the voltage. This provides a method to stop
current flowing into the appliance.

front:
Explain what is meant by
double insulation.
back:
When casing of an appliance is made out of
plastic, it is said to be double insulated since
plastic is an insulator and does not let electricity
pass through.

front: Which connection is not required when the appliance is double insulated? Give a reason for your answer.
back:
Earth wire is not required.
Because earth wire is connected to the casing of the material. If casing is made out of plastic(insulator), earth wire will not be able to let the current flow to the ground.

front:
Circuit breakers can be used instead of fuses.
Give 2 advantages of circuit breakers over
fuses
back:
More sensitive
Easier to reset
Does not need to be replaced.
The change in a wave’s observed wavelength and frequency when there is relative motion between its source and an observer.

front: Describe gamma rays, including uses and issues
back:
High energy electromagnetic radiation emitted from a nucleus.

Used for detecting and treating cancers, and sterilising food and medical implements.

Can cause cell damage and mutations.

They have a very high penetrating power and require several centimetre of lead to absorb them.
The unit of frequency.

A type of radiation that all objects emit and absorb. The hotter an object
is, the greater the infrared radiation it emits in a given time.

The angle of incidence must always equal the angle of reflection when a
wave reflects.

A visual representation of the path of a wave, usually around the point where
it meets a boundary. Rays are usually drawn as straight lines with an arrow pointing in their
direction of travel.
The bouncing back of a wave at a boundary

The ratio of the speed of the wave in a vacuum to the speed of the wave
in a given medium.

The longitudinal waves responsible for sound. They require a medium to
travel through and are transmitted by the vibrations of the medium’s particles.

The velocity at which energy is transferred through the medium. It is equal to
the product of the wave’s wavelength and frequency.

A process of energy transfer through oscillations, without matter being transferred
with it.

An imaginary surface representing points of a wave that are at the same point in
their cycle.

The distance from a point on one wave to the same point on the adjacent wave
(ie. peak to peak or trough to trough).
Waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter.

front: Define frequency and give its units.
back:
● The number of waves passing through a point per second.
● Hz (hertz)

● The maximum displacement of the wave from its equilibrium position.

● The distance between the centre of the wave and a peak

front:
What is meant by the period of the
wave?
back:
The length of time it takes for one full
wave to pass through a point .

front:
What is a longitudinal wave? Give some
examples.
back:
● Vibrations/oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer(wave)

● Examples include sound waves and earthquakes (seismic waves)

front:
What is a transverse wave? Give some
examples.
back:
● A wave with oscillations that are perpendicular (90 degrees) to the direction of energy transfer.

● Examples include electromagnetic waves, water waves

front:
At what speed does an electromagnetic
wave travel in a vacuum?
back: 3 x10<sup>8</sup> m/s

front:
What are the four common properties of all
electromagnetic waves?
back:
· They are all transverse waves
· They all transfer energy or information
· They all travel at the speed of light in vacuum
· They all can be reflected, refracted or diffracted

front:
Which part of the electromagnetic
spectrum has the longest wavelength?
back: Radio waves

front:
Order the electromagnetic spectrum from
the highest frequency to the lowest
frequency.
back:
Gamma rays, x-rays, ultraviolet, visible
light, infrared, microwaves and radio
waves

front:
What are the colours of the visible light
spectrum?
back:
Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue,
Violet.

back: Violet

front: Which colour has the lowest frequency?
back: Red

front: Which colour has the lowest wavelength?
back: Violet

front: Which colour has the highest wavelength?
back: Red

front: What are the uses of radio waves?
back:
● For communication through radio
● Used for satellite transmissions

● Cooking in microwaves ovens
● Communications
● Satellites

front:
Which part of the electromagnetic
spectrum is used in cooking, thermal
imaging and television remote controls?
back: Infrared

front: Give examples of uses for visible light
back:
● Allows us to see (used for vision)
● Photography
● Optical Fibres
(endoscope, communication)

front:
What part of the electromagnetic
spectrum is used for security marking
and in fluorescent lamps?
back: Ultraviolet

front: What are some uses of x-rays?
back:
● Scanners at airports
● Medical x-ray machines

front:
What are the disadvantages of
microwaves?
back:
They can cause heating of internal
tissues in the body

front:
Which part of the electromagnetic
spectrum is used in TV remotes and can
also cause skin burns?
back: Infrared

front:
Does the danger that is associated with
electromagnetic waves increase with
frequency or with wavelength?
back: With frequency

front:
What are the dangers of excessive
exposure to ultraviolet?
back:
You could damage your eyes and the
cells on the surface of your skin. This
could lead to skin cancer or eye
conditions.

front:
What is the normal (in terms of reflection
and refraction)?
back:
A vertical imaginary line which is
perpendicular to the boundary.

front:
What happens when light is refracted
while passing through 2 different media?
back:
● The light changes speed and direction in the new medium
● If the new medium is more dense, the light will travel slower and bend towards the normal
● If the new medium is less dense, the light will travel faster and bend away from the normal
The angle of incidence which causes the angle of reflection to be 90 degrees so that that the light refracts onto the boundary.

When light is trying to pass from a less dense
medium to a denser medium, it can be reflected
back to the less dense medium if the angle of

two media.

front: State two uses of total internal reflection
back:
Any two of:
- Endoscopes
- Periscopes
- Optical Fibres
- Cat Eye Reflectors
- Shining of Diamonds

boundaries and their echoes are detected. The speed of the

boundary (the distance calculated would be double the actual

strength at that point.

front: State the 8 main stores of energy
back:
• Kinetic
  • Gravitational
  • Thermal
  • Chemical
  • Elastic
  • Magnetic
  • Electrostatic
  • Nuclear

front:
What are the four main transfer types between
energy stores?
back:
- Mechanically (or forces)
- Electrically
- By heating
- By radiation (light and sound)

front:
What changes are involved when a ball
(initially stationary) rolls down a hill?
back:
● GPE turns into KE as it rolls downwards

● The speed will increase as the vertical height decreases

● The energy that is not used by the device for its desired purpose is the waste energy.

● An example is a kettle: when energy is changed to sound energy it is classed as waste energy since it is not being used to heat the water.

front: Explain why electrical heater of a kettle is placed at the bottom
back: Heat is mainly transferred by convection within fluids. When a part of the liquid is heated, it expands and becomes less dense therefore it rises up within the fluid. Colder part of the liquid is now denser so it sinks down within the liquid and this forms a convection current when heater is placed at the bottom.

front:
How does the thickness of a building’s walls
affect the rate of cooling?
back:
The thicker the building walls are the further heat
has to travel to escape, hence as you increase
the thickness you decrease the rate of cooling.

front:
How does the thermal conductivity of a building’s
walls affect the rate of cooling?
back:
The higher the thermal conductivity the easier it is for
heat to escape, so a higher rate of cooling.

front:
How can you reduce unwanted heat
transfer?
back:
● Insulation in walls and ceilings, this causes the room to be heated up slower or cooled down slower

● Double glazed windows reduces conduction by putting air or vacuum in between

● Curtains to prevent heat loss by radiation etc.

front:
What is the relationship between work
done on an object and energy
transferred to the object?
back: Work Done = Energy Transferred

- The rate at which energy is transferred.

- Work done(energy transferred) per unit of time

front: What is 1 Watt equivlanent to in terms of other units?
back: 1 Watt = 1 joule per second (J/s).

The lowest possible temperature: −273°C or 0K. At this temperature the particles have no
kinetic energy and so are completely stationary.
The mass per unit volume of an object.

The SI unit of temperature, based on an absolute temperature scale; it is proportional to the
average kinetic energy of the molecules.

The unit of pressure, equal to a force of one Newton acting perpendicular to an
area of one metre squared.

The perpendicular force per unit area acting on the surfaces of a
container as a result of the gas particles colliding with it. It acts equally in all directions.
The force acting perpendicular to a surface, per unit area.

A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance. An
increase in temperature will result in an increase in the particles’ kinetic energies and
velocities.

front: How can Pascals be expressed in other units?

In which direction does pressure act in liquids or
gases?
back: It acts in all directions equally

front:
How do you convert between degree
Celsius and Kelvin?

Explain the pressure of a gas in terms of
the motion of particles.
back:
The particles move in random directions. When
they collide with the walls of a container they
exert a force which acts at a right angle to the
container. This causes pressure.

front:
How does changing the temperature of a
gas affect the velocity of the particles?
back:
The higher the temperature, the more
kinetic energy the particles have and
therefore the faster the average velocity
of the particles.

front:
How does temperature affect the
pressure of a gas?
back:
Increasing temperature increases the average
kinetic energy of particles so they move faster.
Therefore particles collide harder and more
frequently. This increases the pressure

front:
Explain how changing the volume of a
gas affects the pressure of the gas
back:
Volume and pressure are inversely proportional
assuming temperature and mass of the gas is kept
constant. Therefore as volume decreases(gas is
compressed) pressure increases; as volume
increases(gas is expanded) pressure decreases

front:
State 2 assumptions you should make while
using P<sub>1</sub> x V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub> x V<sub>2</sub>
back:
- Fixed mass(number of molecules)
- Fixed Temperature

front:
In a bicycle pump, how does pressing
the piston lead to an increase in the
temperature inside the piston?
back:
● Pressing the piston leads to a decrease in volume
● This leads to an increase in pressure
● The particles collide more frequently
● The velocity of the particles increases
● Therefore their temperature will increase

front:
Give an example of how unwanted
energy transfer while heating can be
reduced.
back:
Through using insulation, which prevents
energy being transferred to the
surroundings.

A current-carrying coil of wire in a magnetic field. The two sides of the coil
that are perpendicular to the magnetic field experience forces in opposite directions, causing
rotation.

A solenoid with an iron core. The magnetism of an electromagnet can
be switched on and off, and the strength changed, through varying the current in the
solenoid.

When there is relative motion between a conductor and a magnetic field, a voltage is induced across the ends of the conductor.

A current will flow if this conductor is part of a complete circuit.

A material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in an existing
magnetic field, but loses its magnetism quickly once it is removed. Induced magnetism
always produces attractive forces.
Lines that show the strength and direction of a magnetic field; they never cross.

front: What are magnetically hard materials? Give examples.
back:
Materials that are permanently
magnetised. Examples: iron, cobalt, nickel (or steel, an iron alloy)

Materials that can be temporarily
magnetised by an external magnetic field, but can get demagnetised when the external field is removed. Examples include alloys with lower amounts of iron.

front:
How do the different poles of the
magnet interact?
back: Like poles repel, unlike poles attract each other

A region surrounding a magnet where
other magnets will experience a force.

front:
Which direction do the field lines in a
magnetic field point?
back: From north to south.

front:
Does a high concentration of field lines
mean the field is strong or weak?
back: Strong

front:
How can you produce a uniform
magnetic field?
back: By placing opposite poles of two magnets across each other, you can create a uniform magnetic field where magnetic field lines are separated with a fixed distance between 2 magnets.

front:
How is a plotting compass used to map
out a magnetic field?
back:
● Place a compass (containing a needle magnet) on a piece of paper near the field
● Move the compass to different places on the paper
● Draw an arrow in each position in the same direction as the needle points
● Once you have gathered enough data, you can join the arrows to make a complete field pattern

front:
Use your hand to show Fleming’s Left
Hand rule, stating which finger represent
field quantity.
back:
● Force (thumb)
● Magnetic field (index finger)
● Current (second finger)
● FBI

front:
How can we increase the magnitude of the
force acting on a current-carrying wire inside
a magnetic field?
back:
● Increase the size of the current
● Increase the strength of magnetic field (Use stronger magnet)

front: What is the motor effect and what causes it?
back:
A current carrying wire placed in a magnetic field experiences a force that pushes the wire.

The force is caused by the field of the current carrying wire interacting with the other magnetic field.

● A cone is attached to a coil with an alternating current placed in a magnetic field
● The motor effect causes a force that pushes/pulls the wire/cone, causing it to move in different directions.
● Due to the alternating current, the force causes the cone to vibrate
● This causes pressure variations in the air (sound waves)

front: How are electric motors kept rotating?
back:
A commutator is used. This switches the
current direction every half turn, which
ensures that the coil keeps spinning.

front:
What factors affect the size of an
induced voltage?
back:
● The number of turns on the coil of wire
● How strong the magnetic field is
● How fast you move the magnet

front:
How is electromagnetic induction used in
alternators to generate alternating
current?
back:
A coil of wire rotates in a magnetic field. The
end of this coil is connected to slip rings which
will cause the current to change direction while
rotating. This means a.c is produced.

front:
What is the shape of the magnetic field
created around a straight wire when a
current is running through?
back: It is circular.

front:
What rule can you use to determine the
direction of a current or magnetic field
around a wire?
back:
The right hand rule
  • Grip a wire with the thumb in the direction of current (conventional)
  • The fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic field.

Radiation that is found in small quantities all around

front:
What is meant by an “isotope” of an
element?

Isotopes are atoms of the same element
with same atomic(proton) number and
different mass(neutron) number.

front:
What is the relative masses of a proton,
neutron and electron?
back:
● Proton: 1 
● Neutron: 1 
● Electron: roughly 1/2000

An atom contains the same number of protons as
electrons and neutrons have no charge.

front:
Which types of radiation are emitted from
unstable nuclei?
back:
● Alpha Particles
● β– (beta minus) Particles
● Gamma rays
● Neutron radiation

- Unstable nuclei in rocks (also give out radon gas)
- Radiation used in medicine
- Some is released from food and water
- Living things (plants can absorb radioactive material as they grow and this can be passed on to the animals that eat them)
- Cosmic rays from the sun

front:
State two pieces of equipment which can be
used to detect radiation.
back:
● Geiger-Müller (GM) Detector
● Photographic Film

front:
Order the types of ionising radiations
starting with the least ionising to most
ionising
back: Gamma → Beta → Alpha

front:
Order the types of ionising radiation,
starting with the most penetrating first.
back: Gamma → Beta → Alpha

front:
When alpha decay occurs, what
happens to the atomic number and the
mass number of the atom?
back:
- The atomic number decreases by 2

- The mass number decreases by 4 (a new element is made)

front:
What effect does releasing gamma
radiation have on the mass number and
atomic number of an atom?
back: No effect

front:
What effect does beta minus decay have
on the mass number and atomic number
of an atom?
back:
● The mass number stays the same as the combined number of neutrons and protons hasn’t changed (one has just turned in the other).

● The atomic number increases since there is one more proton.

front:
What happens in the atom to cause
gamma rays to be released?
back:
When the nucleus decays some of the
nuclei rearranges itself so there is an excess
energy. This may lead to it releasing this
energy in the form of gamma rays.

front:
How does the activity of a radioactive
source decrease over a period of time?
back:
It decreases by a constant ratio over constant
time periods. For example, every 10 minutes a
sample of a radioactive substance may
quarter its activity

front: What is the unit for activity?
back: Becquerel (Bq)

front:
Can you predict when a nucleus will
decay?
back: No, the process is a random process.

front: Give 3 examples of uses of radioactivity.
back:
- Household fire alarms (smoke)
- Irradiating food
- Sterilisation of equipment
- Tracing and gauging thicknesses of materials
- Diagnosis and treatment of cancer

● A radioactive substance in the alarm emits alpha radiation
● Alpha ionises air in the detector,  causing a current to flow between the plates
● Smoke interferes with the radiation; air is no longer ionised and so no current can flow
● This reduction in current flow triggers the alarm

front: How is radiation used in medicine?
back:
● To sterilise equipment: Gamma radiation can kill bacteria cells

● To help treat cancer, as it as it can be used to kill cancer cells

front:
How is beta radiation used to determine
thickness?
back:
● A beta source is placed above the material and a detector is placed below it

● If a lot of radiation is detected by the detector, too much radiation is passing through the material, and so it is too thin

● If only a little radiation is detected, then the material blocks too much radiation, and so it is too thick

front:
What precautions should people take
when using ionising radiation?
back:
● Avoid handling the source directly (use tongs)
● Wear radiation protective clothing
● Keep the radiation in lead containers to reduce the amount of radiation that can escape
● Avoid being exposed to the radiation for long periods of time

front:
Does a long half life or a short half life
make a source more dangerous?
back:
If it has a long half life then it would
remain highly radioactive for longer
therefore making it more dangerous.

front:
What is the difference between
contamination and irradiation?
back:
● Contamination is when radioactive substances are transferred to objects through processes such as touching the source or breathing it in

● Irradiation is when the object comes in contact with the radioactive source. The source doesn’t actually enter your body and the radiation will stop if you move away from the area.

front:
What is a radioactive tracer used for in
medicine?
back:
● The tracer is placed inside the body (it can be in a drink, eaten or injected)

● The tracer releases gamma radiation which is detected by a detector which moves around the body

● This can then be used to produce a picture of the patient's body

front: Explain the process of fission of U-235.
back:
The U-235 absorbs a neutron which makes it
unstable, this causes it to split into two
daughter nuclei and release two or more
neutrons, as well as releasing energy.

front: What is the job of a moderator?
back:
It slows down the neutrons until they are
travelling at a speed slow enough for
them to be absorbed.

front:
How are control rods used to ensure a
controlled reaction?
back:
● They are raised or lowered so that they absorb fewer or greater neutrons
● The number of neutrons that they absorb determines how many reactions can take place

When two small nuclei fuse together to
form a larger nuclei. This process also
releases energy.

In the sun - stars use fusion as their
energy source

front:
Why can’t nuclear fusion be used as our
energy source?
back:
● On earth we can’t get high temperatures and pressures for nuclear fusion to happen, whilst still being cost effective
● This is because both nuclei are positive therefore a lot of energy is required to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between the two nuclei

Man-made satellites that have been sent into space for purposes such
as satellite imaging and communications.

Objects consisting of rock, dust and ice that travel in the universe at high speeds.
When they approach the sun they vaporise and produce a trail.
A system containing billions of stars.

The stable state of all stars. The gravitational forces pulling the star
together, and the pressure pushing outwards, are balanced.
The galaxy in which our solar system is located.
The moons that orbit planets.

The radius of a body’s orbit. For a stable orbit, a change in its orbital radius
is required for the body to undergo a speed change.

A measure of how fast an object orbits. It is directly proportional to the orbital
radius and inversely proportional to the orbital period.
The time it takes for an object in orbit to complete one full cycle.

The first stage all stars go through after forming from a nebula. In this stage the
star becomes hot enough for hydrogen nuclei to fuse.

When their hydrogen is used up and larger nuclei are produced by fusion,
stars of a similar magnitude to the Sun will expand to form a red giant.
A large system of billions of galaxies.

When the fusion reactions in stars of a similar magnitude to the sun come to
an end, the star will contract under gravity and cool down to form a white dwarf.

front:
Why does your weight vary across
planets?
back:
● Your weight is dependant on g, since weight = mass x g
● The gravitational field strength (g) of a planet varies depending on the radius and mass of the planet
● This means that your weight will also vary

front: What does our solar system consist of?
back:
● The sun (our star)
● 8 Planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune)
● The planet’s natural satellites (ie. the moon)
● Dwarf planets
● Comets and asteroids

front:
Describe the orbits of moons, planets,
comets and artificial satellites.
back:
·Planets follow a (approximately) circular orbit around the Sun.

·Satellites including moons follow a (approximately) circular orbit around planets.

·Comets follow elliptical orbits around the Sun.

front:
Which force is makes astronomical objects
follow orbits?
back:
Gravitational force pulls the objects
causing them to follow orbits around
massive objects.

front:
Stars can be classified according to colour.
Order the given colours of stars from coldest to
hottest:
● Yellow
● Blue
● Red
● White
● Orange
back:
Coldest → Hottest
Red → Orange → Yellow → White → Blue

front: Which stage is the Sun currently in?
back: Main sequence
A cloud of gas and dust in space

front:
Describe the transition of the star from
the nebula stage to the main sequence.
back:
● The nebula increases in size until it is pulled in due to its gravity, causing GPE to turn into KE of molecules

● As it gets smaller, particles move faster and collide harder so temperature increases.

● Eventually the nebula will become dense and hot enough to begin fusion

front:
What occurs in the stage when a star is
a main sequence star?
back:
● The fusion in the star releases energy

● During fusion, main sequence stars mostly turn hydrogen into helium.

● Thermal energy released from fusion causes an outward pressure which balances the inward pressure caused by gravity

● The star is in equilibrium so will not collapse due to gravity or expand due to fusion. It is stable.

front:
What happens when a star transitions to
the red giant stage?
back:
● Once all of the hydrogen fuel has been used up, the star begins to fuse helium and other larger nuclei

● This causes the star to expand and become a red giant

front:
How does a star become a white dwarf
from a red giant?
back:
● Once all reactions have taken place, the star’s gravity pulls in all of its mass, making a small, dense white dwarf

● This will cool down to form a black dwarf

front:
What stages occur for the evolution of
stars that have a mass which is larger
than the sun?
back:
- Nebula
- Main sequence star
- Red supergiant star
- Supernova
- Black hole/ neutron star

After the red supergiant stage the star will
expand and get hotter, eventually it will explode
as a supernova. What is left turns into a neutron
star (or a black hole if it is very large).
